entities.name: Church of England
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Church of England, established in 1534 when Henry VIII's Act of Supremacy declared the English monarch head of the English Church rather than the Pope, is the world's third-largest Christian denomination (85 million members in 165 countries through the Anglican Communion) and the established national church of England — its 26 bishops sitting by right in the House of Lords (Lords Spiritual) as the only religious body with reserved parliamentary seats in any modern democracy. The Church of England's establishment bridged Catholic tradition and Protestant theology through the 'via media' principle, creating a distinctive Anglican identity.

Henry VIII's break with Rome was motivated by his desire to annul his marriage to Catherine of Aragon — Pope Clement VII refused, being effectively a prisoner of Catherine's nephew Emperor Charles V. Archbishop Thomas Cranmer drafted the Book of Common Prayer (1549, revised 1662) — arguably the most influential text in the history of the English language, shaping Shakespeare's vocabulary, the King James Bible's cadences, and the prose style of Lincoln and Churchill. Cranmer was burned at the stake under Mary I before Elizabeth I's Settlement confirmed Protestantism.

The Church of England's 39 Articles (1563) defined Anglican theology as Reformed Catholic — maintaining bishops, liturgy, and sacraments from Catholic tradition while rejecting papal authority and affirming Protestant justification by faith. The Archbishop of Canterbury serves as 'first among equals' in the 165-country Anglican Communion. The 1994 decision to ordain women priests and 2014 women bishops caused ongoing tensions; the 2023 Prayers of Love and Faith for same-sex couples provoked a threatened Global South Anglican schism.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Church of England's Book of Common Prayer shaped the English language more than any text except the Bible — its cadences appear in Shakespeare, Lincoln's Gettysburg Address, and Churchill's wartime speeches — making it the theological institution with the greatest literary and linguistic influence in history.
